# SLAI Knowledge Bundle

Strategic knowledge encoded for the `sts2-coach` Skill. Paraphrases publicly available content from **Baalorlord** ([Twitch](https://www.twitch.tv/baalorlord), [YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/@baalorlord)). Any misrepresentation is ours, not his — see ATTRIBUTION.md.

# General Strategy

## Four Pillars

Baalorlord's four fundamental pillars that every successful deck must address. A deck that is weak in any pillar will struggle. Evaluate your deck against these pillars after every card reward and shop visit.

### Damage Output

Your ability to deal damage to enemies. Split into two sub-categories: frontloaded damage and scaling damage. You need BOTH — frontloaded for hallway fights and early turns, scaling for long boss fights.

#### Frontload

Damage you can deal in the first 1-2 turns of combat without any setup. This is your bread and butter for hallway fights and the early turns of elite/boss fights.

**Importance:** Critical in Act 1 where you have no scaling yet. Hallway fights should ideally end in 2-3 turns. If fights drag on, you take unnecessary damage that limits your pathing options.

**Target:** Aim to deal 30-40+ damage in the first 2 turns by mid-Act 1. By Act 2, you want 50+ frontloaded damage available.

##### Examples

- Ironclad: Carnage, Pummel, Uppercut, Headbutt
- Silent: Backstab, Predator, Dash, Poisoned Stab
- Defect: Cold Snap, Ball Lightning, Doom and Gloom, Compile Driver
- Necrobinder: Osty attacks, Doom application cards
- Regent: Sovereign Blade (with Forge stacks), Star-powered attacks

**Common Mistake:** Ignoring frontload in favor of scaling. A deck full of scaling cards with no frontload will lose 30+ HP in hallway fights before the scaling comes online.

#### Scaling

Damage that grows over the course of a fight. Strength, Poison stacks, Focus + Orbs, Doom accumulation, Forge stacks — anything that makes each subsequent turn deal more damage than the last.

**Importance:** Essential for boss fights and tough elites that last 5+ turns. Without scaling, bosses become wars of attrition you will lose. The longer a fight goes, the more scaling matters.

**Target:** Have at least one reliable scaling source by the end of Act 1. By Act 2, you want 2+ scaling sources or one very strong one.

##### Examples

- Ironclad: Demon Form, Inflame, Spot Weakness, Limit Break
- Silent: Noxious Fumes, Catalyst, Envenom
- Defect: Defragment, Biased Cognition, Capacitor, Echo Form
- Necrobinder: Doom stacking, recurring Souls
- Regent: Star generation engines, Forge accumulation

**Common Mistake:** Over-investing in scaling without enough block or frontload. A Demon Form is worthless if you die on turn 2.

### Cycle Time

How quickly you see your important cards again. Cycle time is determined by deck size, draw, and card manipulation. A smaller, tighter deck with good draw sees its power cards every 2 turns instead of every 4.

**Ideal Deck Size:** 20-25 cards for most builds. Some exhaust-heavy builds can go larger (28-32) because they thin in combat. Some ultra-thin builds work at 15-18 but require specific synergies.

**Target Cycle:** See your full deck every ~2 turns. With a 20-card deck and 5-card hand, you see everything in 4 draws (2 turns). Add draw cards and it's even faster.

#### Calculation Formula

**Formula:** cycle_time_in_turns = (total_deck_size - net_extra_draw_per_turn) / cards_drawn_per_turn

**Default Cards Drawn Per Turn:** 5

##### Examples

**10 Card Starter:** 10 / 5 = 2-turn cycle time

**20 Card Deck No Extra Draw:** 20 / 5 = 4-turn cycle time

**20 Card Deck With 2 Draw Powers:** (20 - 4) / 5 = 3.2-turn cycle time

**30 Card Deck No Draw:** 30 / 5 = 6-turn cycle time (DANGER — your scaling card might appear only once in a 6-turn fight)

**Key Insight:** Cantrips (cards that draw exactly 1 card, like Quick Slash) are CYCLE-NEUTRAL — they replace themselves. Cards that draw 2+ are cycle-POSITIVE — they shrink effective deck size every play.

**Why It Matters:** If your deck has 35 cards and your win condition is 3 specific cards, you might not see them together for 5+ turns. That's 5 turns of taking damage without your engine running.

#### Tips

- Skip card rewards more often than you take them — every card you add increases cycle time
- Prioritize draw cards: they effectively reduce your deck size by letting you see more cards per turn
- Remove Strikes and Defends at every opportunity — they are the weakest cards in your deck
- Exhaust cards naturally thin your deck during combat, improving cycle time as the fight progresses
- Innate cards reduce effective cycle time by guaranteeing key cards in opening hand
- Retain cards improve consistency by letting you hold key cards across turns

#### Card Removal Priority

- Strikes first (they deal less damage than almost any common attack)
- Defends second (they block less than almost any common skill)
- Curses/Status immediately when possible
- Redundant copies of conditional cards

### Block Density

The percentage of your deck that can generate block. You need enough block cards to survive enemy attacks on most turns, but not so many that you can't kill enemies.

**Target Percentage:** 33

**Target Description:** Roughly 1 in 3 cards should generate block. In a 21-card deck, that's ~7 block cards. This ensures you draw at least 1-2 block cards per hand.

#### The 33 Percent Math

**Starter Deck Baseline:** Starter decks typically sit at 40-50% block density (4 Defends out of 10 cards = 40%)

**Target:** Exactly 33% block density (e.g., 10 block cards in a 30-card deck)

**Why Exactly 33:** At 33%, you have an 89.1% chance to draw AT LEAST 1 block card per turn, and a 55.1% chance to draw 2 or more. That's enough block coverage without clogging your hand on turns the enemy is BUFFING (and you don't need block).

**Above 33 Diminishing Returns:** Above ~40%, you start drawing too many block cards on turns when block is wasted. Your damage suffers without proportional defense gain.

**Below 33 Risky:** Below 25%, you'll have block-less hands often enough that one bad shuffle gets you killed.

**Card Draw Lets You Lower Target:** Higher card draw engines (like Defect's Hologram or Silent's Storm of Steel) let you lower overall Block Density safely, because larger effective hand sizes naturally guarantee defensive options.

#### Tips

- Block cards that also do something else (Shrug It Off draws, Dash blocks AND attacks) are premium picks
- Don't neglect block in Act 1 — you need to survive elites and the Act 1 boss
- Strength/scaling builds still need block; you can't just race bosses
- Artifact and Intangible are the best 'block' in the game — they prevent damage entirely
- Calculate how much incoming damage you expect and whether your block density can handle it
- Dexterity increases the value of every block card — it's block scaling

#### Scaling Block

Block that grows over time, similar to damage scaling. Dexterity, Metallicize, After Image, Frost Orbs with Focus — these make your block better every turn.

##### Examples

- Ironclad: Barricade + Body Slam, Metallicize, Feel No Pain
- Silent: Footwork (Dexterity), After Image, Blur
- Defect: Frost Orbs + Focus, Glacier, Reinforced Body
- Necrobinder: Osty as meat shield, defensive Souls
- Regent: Star-powered block generation

### Upgrade Density

The percentage of your deck that is upgraded. Upgraded cards are significantly more efficient — they deal more damage, block more, cost less, or gain additional effects. Campfires are your primary upgrade source.

**Target Percentage:** 50

**Target Description:** Aim to have at least half your deck upgraded by Act 2. By Act 3, 60-75% upgraded is ideal. Upgrades are one of the most reliable ways to increase deck power.

#### Tips

- Upgrading is almost always better than resting at a campfire if you're above 50% HP
- Prioritize upgrading your most-played cards — cards you see every fight benefit most from upgrades
- Some upgrades are transformative: Bash+ applies 3 Vulnerable, Neutralize+ applies 2 Weak, etc.
- Calculate the total value of an upgrade over an entire run — an upgraded card played 50+ times adds up enormously
- Key upgrades that change card function (add draw, reduce cost, add effects) are highest priority
- Upgrades to 0-cost cards are often very efficient since you always play them

#### Upgrade Priority Framework

- 1. Cards that gain new effects when upgraded (cost reduction, added draw, new mechanics)
- 2. Cards you play every single turn (your most consistent damage/block sources)
- 3. Scaling cards (making your scaling faster or stronger compounds over a fight)
- 4. Cards that go from situational to always-good when upgraded
- 5. Cards with minor stat bumps (last priority — +3 damage is less impactful than a new effect)

## Card Evaluation

How to evaluate card rewards and decide what to take, skip, or remove.

### Jobs Framework

Baalorlord's 'Jobs' framework for card evaluation. Every card should fill a specific job your deck needs. Don't evaluate cards in a vacuum — evaluate them based on what your deck is currently missing.

#### Jobs

Deal immediate damage without setup

**Job:** Frontload Damage

**When Needed:** Always needed in Act 1. Check if your first 2 turns deal enough damage to kill small hallway enemies.


Grow damage output over a long fight

**Job:** Scaling Damage

**When Needed:** Needed before first elite, critical before first boss. If you have no scaling, prioritize this.


Prevent incoming damage

**Job:** Block Generation

**When Needed:** Always needed. If less than ~30% of your deck generates block, prioritize block cards.


See more cards per turn, improve consistency

**Job:** Card Draw

**When Needed:** Needed once deck size exceeds 20 cards. Critical if you have powerful cards you rarely see.


Handle multiple-enemy encounters efficiently

**Job:** AOE Damage

**When Needed:** Need at least 1 AOE source by mid-Act 1. Multiple enemy fights are common and dangerous.


Weak, Vulnerable, or other debuffs that reduce enemy effectiveness

**Job:** Enemy Debuffs

**When Needed:** Weak is always valuable (reduces damage by 25%). Vulnerable amplifies your damage by 50%.


Scry, retain, search, or otherwise control what you draw

**Job:** Deck Manipulation

**When Needed:** Becomes important in Act 2+ as fights become more complex and sequencing matters more.


#### Evaluation Process

- 1. Identify which jobs your deck currently needs most urgently
- 2. Evaluate each card reward by which job(s) it fills
- 3. Prefer cards that fill multiple jobs simultaneously (e.g., Shrug It Off blocks AND draws)
- 4. Skip the reward if no card fills a needed job — adding bloat is worse than skipping
- 5. Consider the next 3-5 fights: what do you need to survive RIGHT NOW?

### Two Cost Cards

Baalorlord emphasizes that new players chronically undervalue 2-cost cards. A 2-cost card that does 2 things is often more efficient than playing two 1-cost cards that each do one thing.

**Reasoning:** A 2-cost card takes 1 card slot in your hand and 1 draw to see. Two 1-cost cards take 2 slots and 2 draws. The 2-cost card is better for cycle time even if the raw numbers seem similar.

#### Examples

- Carnage (2 cost, 20 damage) vs two Strikes (2 cost total, 12 damage) — Carnage wins on damage AND cycle time
- Dash (2 cost, 10 damage + 10 block) replaces a Strike AND a Defend in one card slot
- Doom and Gloom (2 cost, 10 damage + channel Dark orb) provides damage AND orb value in one play

#### When To Avoid Two Cost

- When you have very limited energy (3 energy with no energy relics)
- When the 2-cost card's effect is too situational or conditional
- When you already have too many 2-cost cards and can't play your full hand

### Skipping Philosophy

One of Baalorlord's most important teachings: skipping card rewards is a powerful strategic tool. Most players take too many cards.

#### Key Principles

- Every card you add to your deck increases cycle time — make sure it's worth it
- A mediocre card is WORSE than no card because it dilutes your draws
- In Act 2 and Act 3, you should be skipping 40-60% of card rewards
- Ask yourself: 'Does this card make my deck better, or just bigger?'
- The best players skip aggressively and have tight, focused decks
- It's better to have a 20-card deck where every card is good than a 30-card deck with 10 filler cards

#### When To Take

- The card fills an urgent job your deck needs
- The card has exceptional synergy with your existing cards
- You're in Act 1 and need any reasonable damage or block
- The card is a rare/powerful card you'd build around

#### When To Skip

- No card fills an urgent need
- The cards are marginal upgrades over what you already have
- Your deck is already 25+ cards and you don't have exhaust mechanics
- Taking the card would reduce your consistency more than it adds power

## Resource Management

### Hp As Resource

Baalorlord's core teaching: HP is a resource to be SPENT, not hoarded. Taking 5 damage in a hallway fight to end it 1 turn faster is often correct because it saves you from taking 10 damage over 2 additional turns.

#### Key Principles

- HP is a resource, not a score — spending HP efficiently is a skill
- Taking damage to end fights faster is often correct (less total damage taken)
- Low HP forces bad pathing — maintaining 50%+ HP gives you options
- Resting at campfires is almost always wrong if you're above 50% HP — upgrade instead
- Elite fights are worth the HP investment if you can afford it — the rewards are massive

#### Hp Thresholds

**Comfortable:** 70%+ HP — take any fight, hunt elites freely

**Moderate:** 50-70% HP — still take elites if your deck is strong, otherwise play safe

**Danger:** 30-50% HP — avoid elites, consider resting at campfires

**Critical:** Below 30% HP — rest at every campfire, take safest possible path, use potions liberally

### Potion Usage

Baalorlord strongly advocates using potions aggressively, especially on elites. Hoarding potions for the boss is one of the most common mistakes.

#### Key Principles

- Use potions on elites — elite rewards (relics, extra cards, gold) are worth more than saving potions
- A potion used to take 0 damage from an elite is better than saving it for a boss where you'd take 10 damage anyway
- Potions are free power — there is no cost to using them except opportunity cost of a better use later
- You will find more potions — don't hoard them
- If you have 3+ potions going into an elite, use at least 1-2
- The only time to save potions is if you're about to fight a boss and your deck genuinely needs the help

#### Potion Priority

- Use offensive potions (Strength, Fire, Attack potions) on elites to kill them faster
- Use defensive potions (Block, Fairy in a Bottle) when you'd otherwise take lethal or near-lethal damage
- Smoke Bomb is an emergency escape — use it if a fight is going badly and you'd lose 40+ HP
- Entropic Brew / Fruit Juice are best used before tough fights to maximize their value

### Gold Management

Gold is valuable but should be spent strategically. Don't hoard gold — spend it at shops on high-impact purchases.

#### Key Principles

- Card removal is almost always worth the gold — removing a Strike or Defend improves every future fight
- Relics from shops can be game-changing — evaluate them against your deck's needs
- Don't buy cards from shops unless they fill a critical need — card rewards are free
- Save 300-400+ gold for a shop visit for maximum value
- Prioritize: Card Removal > Key Relics > Potions > Cards

#### Shop Priority

- 1. Card removal (always buy at least one removal per shop visit)
- 2. High-synergy relics that complement your deck
- 3. Potions if you're about to fight an elite or boss
- 4. Cards only if they fill a critical gap in your deck
- 5. Colorless cards if they're premium (Apotheosis, Master of Strategy, etc.)

## Act Transitions

What your deck should look like at each stage of the run.

### Act1 Exit

**Deck Size:** 15-20 cards

#### Requirements

- At least 1 scaling source
- Enough frontload to kill hallway enemies in 2-3 turns
- Some block generation beyond starting Defends
- 1-2 card removals completed
- At least 3-4 upgrades

### Act2 Exit

**Deck Size:** 20-25 cards

#### Requirements

- Strong scaling that works reliably
- Good block density (~33%)
- AOE capability for multi-enemy fights
- 50%+ cards upgraded
- Core synergies established

### Act3 Entry

**Focus:** Consolidation and optimization

#### Requirements

- Deck is mostly complete — skip most card rewards
- Focus on upgrades and card removal
- Prepare specifically for the Act 3 boss
- Ensure you have answers for the toughest fights

## Meta Principles

**Adaptability:** Never force a build. Adapt to what the game offers you. The best players build around the cards and relics they find, not the archetype they wanted.

**Information Usage:** Use all available information: upcoming enemies, map layout, boss identity, current HP, potion slots. Every decision should incorporate known information.

**Risk Assessment:** Every decision involves risk. Calculate expected outcomes: 'If I take this elite path, I gain a relic but might lose 20 HP. Is that worth it given my current state?'

**Long Term Thinking:** Don't optimize for the current fight — optimize for the current ACT. A card that's bad now but great for the boss is worth taking if you can survive without it until then.

**Practice Mindset:** Every loss is a learning opportunity. Ask 'What could I have done differently?' after every run. The best players constantly self-evaluate.

# Pathing Strategy

## Hard Pool Vs Easy Pool

STS2 splits hallway fights into two pools — 'easy' and 'hard'. The first encounters of each act are guaranteed easy; later hallway encounters can be hard. Elite players ruthlessly exploit this.

### Guarantees

**Act 1:** First THREE hallway combats are guaranteed easy pool

**Act 2:** First TWO hallway combats are guaranteed easy pool

**Act 3:** First TWO hallway combats are guaranteed easy pool

### Why It Matters

- Easy pool fights cost ~5 HP on average; hard pool fights cost ~10-15 HP and can rival elites
- Farm the easy pool first for cards, gold, and a rest site — THEN tackle elites or question marks
- Minimize hard pool hallway combats before your first rest site each act

**Pathing Implication:** Plan paths that hit the guaranteed easy fights early, then chain into a campfire or shop, THEN engage elites or hard hallways. Going 'shop → elite → elite → boss' with no easy farming is a quick death.

## Bonfires Over Elites

Unlike STS1, BONFIRES (campfires) are king in STS2. Relics from elites are powerful, but upgrades often equal a direct extra energy or massive HP preservation, making bonfires statistically more valuable than risky elite fights.

### The Math

- An elite costs ~15-25 HP and grants 1 relic (variable value) + 1 card + ~60-100 gold
- A campfire costs 0 HP and grants either ~30% HP recovery OR a permanent upgrade (typically +3 damage, +3 block, or a transformative effect)
- Over a 25-card deck, one upgrade on a frequently-played card outvalues most relics

### When Elites Beat Bonfires

- Your deck specifically needs the relic class (energy relics, draw relics, scaling relics)
- You're above 70% HP and below the act's elite count target (2-3 in Act 1)
- The elite is one your deck specifically counters (avoid Desa Millipede with pure burst, etc.)

### When Bonfires Beat Elites

- You have any key card that needs upgrading and HP > 50%
- Your deck is mid-strength (no breakaway scaling, no boss relic) — extra power matters more than another relic
- It's late in the act and your elite count is met

## Shop Discipline

See economy.json for shop strategy in detail. Pathing-relevant rules below.

### Shop Pathing Rules

- Aim for exactly ONE shop per act
- Visit a second shop ONLY if you have 400+ gold and a clear high-value purchase in mind
- Visit shops LATE in the act after farming gold from hallway fights
- Never path through a shop when broke — it wastes a node that could have generated power
- Never end an act with 200+ unspent gold — that's a sign you under-spent at the shop

## Look Ahead Method

Baalorlord's fundamental pathing principle: before choosing a path, look at the ENTIRE act map and plan your route from bottom to top. Don't make node-by-node decisions — plan the whole act.

### Steps

- 1. Look at the boss node at the top — identify what boss you're facing and what your deck needs to beat it
- 2. Identify all elite nodes, campfire nodes, shop nodes, and question mark nodes
- 3. Plan a path that hits the right number of elites for your deck strength (usually 2-3 in Act 1)
- 4. Ensure you hit at least 1 campfire before each elite if possible
- 5. Plan shop visits when you'll have 300+ gold
- 6. Prefer paths with more hallway fights early (card rewards to build your deck) and more campfires/shops late (to prepare for the boss)
- 7. Have a backup path in mind if you take more damage than expected

**Key Insight:** The map is deterministic — you can see exactly what's coming. Use this information. Players who path reactively (choosing at each fork) perform significantly worse than those who plan ahead.

## Campfire Strategy

Campfire decisions (rest vs upgrade vs other options) are among the most impactful decisions in any run.

### Rest Vs Upgrade

**General Rule:** Upgrade is almost always correct if you're above 50% HP. The cumulative value of an upgrade over the rest of the run usually exceeds the HP you'd recover.

#### Rest When

- Below 40% HP and you have tough fights ahead (elites, boss)
- You would die to the next fight without healing
- All your key cards are already upgraded
- You have Regal Pillow (rest heals 15 extra HP) making rest more efficient
- The upcoming path is very dangerous and you need the safety margin

#### Upgrade When

- Above 50% HP
- You have a high-impact card to upgrade (key scaling card, important block card)
- You're early in the act and the upgrade will pay dividends over many fights
- You have healing from other sources (Burning Blood, Feed, relics)

### Upgrade Priority

Which card to upgrade at a campfire. Prioritize cards that gain the most from upgrading.

#### Tier 1 Priority

- Cards that gain new effects (e.g., Bash+ applies 3 Vulnerable instead of 2)
- Cards that reduce cost (2-cost becoming 1-cost is massive)
- Key scaling cards (your primary damage/block engine)
- Cards you play every single combat

#### Tier 2 Priority

- Draw cards (more draw = better consistency)
- Block cards you rely on for survival
- AOE cards before multi-enemy fights

#### Tier 3 Priority

- Minor stat increases (+3 damage, +3 block)
- Situational cards you only play occasionally
- Cards that will be removed soon anyway

### Special Campfire Options

**Lift:** Gain 1 Strength permanently. Take this when you have no high-impact upgrade targets. Compounds with multi-hit attacks.

**Toke:** Remove a card (from Girya or other sources). Excellent for removing Strikes/Defends.

**Dig:** Gain a relic (from Shovel). Always take the relic — relics are permanent power.

## Elite Hunting

Elites are the primary way to gain relics, which are permanent power increases. Hunting elites aggressively is key to strong runs, but you need to manage risk.

### Hp Thresholds

#### Act1

**Safe To Fight:** 60%+ HP (48+ HP for most characters)

**Risky:** 40-60% HP — fight only if your deck is strong or you have potions

**Avoid:** Below 40% HP — the relic isn't worth dying

#### Act2

**Safe To Fight:** 50%+ HP (40+ HP for most characters)

**Risky:** 30-50% HP — only with potions and a strong deck

**Avoid:** Below 30% HP

#### Act3

**Safe To Fight:** 50%+ HP with a well-built deck

**Risky:** 30-50% HP — consider your deck's matchup against the specific elite

**Avoid:** Below 30% HP — focus on reaching the boss healthy

### Target Elites Per Act

**Act1:** 2-3 elites. You need relics to snowball your run. 1 elite is too few, 4 is greedy.

**Act2:** 2-3 elites. Continue building relic advantage. Act 2 elites are harder but rewards are proportionally better.

**Act3:** 1-2 elites. Be more selective — you're preparing for the final boss, not building your deck.

### Elite Specific Strategies

#### Byrdonis

Flying enemy that alternates between attacking and buffing. Can stack Strength quickly.

**Key Counter:** Kill fast before Strength stacks become overwhelming. Frontloaded damage is king.

**Danger Level:** Medium — predictable pattern but punishes slow decks

##### Tips

- Apply Weak to reduce its attack damage significantly
- Prioritize damage over block in the first 2 turns
- If it buffs, you have one turn to deal major damage before the buffed attack hits

#### Entomancer

Summons minions that attack independently. Can overwhelm you with multiple damage sources.

**Key Counter:** AOE damage to clear minions. Focus the Entomancer itself when minions are dead.

**Danger Level:** High — multiple damage sources are hard to block against

##### Tips

- AOE is essential — without it, minions will chip you down
- Kill minions first, then focus the Entomancer
- Block is less effective because damage comes from multiple sources
- Potions are very valuable here if you lack AOE

#### Decimillipede

Multi-hitting enemy that benefits from long fights. Applies debuffs and scales over time.

**Key Counter:** End the fight quickly. Scaling damage and strong frontload.

**Danger Level:** Medium-High — gets worse the longer the fight goes

##### Tips

- This is a race — kill it before its scaling overwhelms your block
- Strength and damage scaling are your best friends here
- Artifact can prevent its debuffs from sticking
- Don't try to out-block it long-term; focus on offense

#### Infested Prism

Tanky elite with high HP. May spawn minions or have damage reflection mechanics.

**Key Counter:** Sustained damage output and patience. This is a longer fight.

**Danger Level:** Medium — not as bursty but punishes low-damage decks

##### Tips

- Scaling is very important for this fight due to high enemy HP
- Maintain block consistency throughout the fight
- Poison and other damage-over-time effects are very effective
- Don't rush — this fight rewards steady play

## Shop Timing

Shops are valuable for card removal, relics, and potions. Time your shop visits to maximize gold efficiency.

### Optimal Timing

**Frequency:** Visit ~1 shop per act. More if you have excess gold, fewer if you're gold-starved.

**When To Visit:** Late in the act when you've accumulated gold from fights. Aim to have 300-400+ gold when you hit a shop.

**Avoid:** Don't visit shops with less than 150 gold — you won't be able to afford anything impactful.

### Shop Priorities

#### Always Buy

- Card removal (75-100 gold, increasing per removal) — removing a Strike/Defend improves EVERY future fight
- High-synergy relics that directly complement your deck strategy
- Emergency potions if you're about to fight a tough elite/boss and need help

#### Usually Buy

- Strong colorless cards (Apotheosis, Master of Strategy, Panacea)
- Key missing pieces for your deck (e.g., AOE if you have none)
- Relics with broad utility (energy relics, draw relics)

#### Sometimes Buy

- Cards that fill a secondary need
- Potions for the boss fight
- Situational relics

#### Rarely Buy

- Cards you could get from rewards
- Niche relics with limited application
- Anything when you're low on gold and have more shops ahead

### Gold Earning Tips

- Take gold rewards from fights when you don't need the card or potion
- Question mark events sometimes give gold
- Selling potions at shops if you have excess
- Some relics generate gold passively

## Boss Preparation

Preparing for the act boss is a key part of pathing. You can see which boss you'll face from the start of the act.

### General Approach

- Check the boss icon at the start of each act
- Counter-draft: pick cards that specifically address the boss's mechanics
- Ensure your deck has both damage scaling and block for the boss fight
- Use the last 2-3 fights before the boss to fine-tune (upgrade, remove cards, use events)

### Pre Boss Checklist

- Do I have enough scaling to win a 10+ turn fight?
- Do I have enough block to survive the boss's damage output?
- Do I have an answer for the boss's specific mechanics?
- Am I above 50% HP? If not, should I rest at the next campfire?
- Do I have potions that will help in this specific fight?
- Have I removed enough Strikes/Defends to keep my deck consistent?

## Act By Act Guidance

### Act1

**Theme:** Build Your Deck — Establish your foundation

**Primary Goal:** Get enough cards to beat the Act 1 boss. Focus on frontloaded damage and basic scaling.

#### Pathing Priorities

- Take early hallway fights for card rewards — you need cards to build your deck
- Fight 2-3 elites for relics (relics are permanent power)
- Hit at least 1 campfire for an upgrade before the boss
- Visit a shop if you have 250+ gold (card removal is critical)
- Question marks are fine but hallway fights are often better in Act 1 (guaranteed card rewards)

**Card Taking:** Take cards somewhat liberally in Act 1. You need to fill jobs (damage, block, scaling). Be pickier as you approach the boss.

**Common Act1 Mistake:** Being too greedy with elites. If your deck isn't ready for an elite, the relic isn't worth 40+ HP of damage.

### Act2

**Theme:** Refine Your Deck — Solidify your strategy

**Primary Goal:** Establish your core synergies and scaling. Your deck should have a clear identity by the end of Act 2.

#### Pathing Priorities

- Continue fighting elites (2-3) for relics
- Prioritize campfires for upgrades — upgraded cards scale your power significantly
- Shop visits are important for card removal and key relics
- Start being more selective with card rewards — skip anything that doesn't fit your strategy
- Question marks can provide valuable events (card transforms, relics, etc.)

**Card Taking:** Be much pickier than Act 1. Only take cards that directly strengthen your core strategy or fill a critical weakness.

**Common Act2 Mistake:** Taking too many cards. Your deck should be 20-25 cards by end of Act 2. Every card you add increases cycle time.

### Act3

**Theme:** Consolidate — Prepare for the final boss

**Primary Goal:** Optimize your existing deck through upgrades and removals. Skip most card rewards.

#### Pathing Priorities

- Fight 1-2 elites if you're healthy and your deck handles them well
- Campfires for upgrades are very valuable — every upgrade matters for the final boss
- Final shop visit for last-chance card removal or critical purchases
- Avoid unnecessary damage — reaching the boss healthy is paramount
- Plan your path to the boss with maximum campfires and minimum risk

**Card Taking:** Skip 60%+ of card rewards. Your deck is built — focus on making it better, not bigger.

**Common Act3 Mistake:** Still taking cards. Your deck is nearly complete. Adding more cards dilutes your best cards.

## Risk Management

How to assess and manage risk during pathing decisions.

### Risk Factors

- Current HP percentage — lower HP = higher risk
- Deck strength — stronger decks can handle riskier paths
- Available potions — potions provide a safety net for tough fights
- Upcoming nodes — know what's coming before you commit to a path
- Act progression — more risk is acceptable early in an act, less acceptable near the boss

### Risk Mitigation

- Always have a backup path planned
- Keep potions for emergencies (but don't hoard them — use on elites)
- Rest at campfires when below 40% HP with tough fights ahead
- Take safer paths when your deck has clear weaknesses
- Smoke Bomb potion is an emergency escape from a fight going badly

### Hp Threshold Guidance

**Above 70:** Play aggressively — hunt elites, take risks, upgrade at campfires

**50 To 70:** Play normally — take elites if your deck is ready, upgrade when safe

**30 To 50:** Play carefully — avoid elites without potions, consider resting

**Below 30:** Play defensively — rest at every campfire, take the safest path, use potions liberally

## Question Mark Strategy

Question mark nodes (unknown events) can provide card transforms, relics, gold, healing, card removal, or sometimes negative effects.

### When To Prioritize

- When you need healing but don't want to waste a campfire resting
- When you're looking for card transforms or unusual options
- When hallway fights aren't giving you useful card rewards
- When you have relics that benefit from events (e.g., Ssserpent Head)

### When To Avoid

- When you desperately need specific card rewards (hallway fights are more reliable)
- When you can't afford any negative event outcomes
- When you need guaranteed combat encounters for gold or card rewards

### Tips

- Many events are beneficial — don't fear question marks
- Some events offer free card removal, which is extremely valuable
- Events that offer max HP increases are almost always worth taking
- Card transform events can turn bad cards into great ones (or vice versa — risk/reward)

# Combat Micro

Per-turn micro-decisions in combat. The macro stuff (pillars, pathing, drafting) is half the game; the other half is making the right play sequence every turn. This file is the grandmaster's mental checklist.

## Turn 1 Checklist

Before playing a single card on turn 1, the grandmaster runs through this five-step mental checklist. Slowing down here saves more HP across the run than any other habit.

### Steps

#### Check the draw pile

**Step:** 1

**What:** Open the draw pile view. Identify what you'll likely draw next turn. Are there key cards (scaling powers, AOE, big block) you should plan to play?

**Why:** Determines whether you should save energy this turn for a bigger play next turn, or spend everything now.


#### Check enemy intent

**Step:** 2

**What:** Read every enemy's intent icon. Multi-hits, debuffs, buff intents, sleep, charging — each shapes your play differently.

##### Key Signals

- Multi-hit (2x or 3x attack) → block matters more than usual; Weak or Vulnerable scales further
- Debuff intent → consider Artifact stacks or rushing the kill
- Self-buff intent → kill the enemy NOW before the buff lands
- Sleep / charging → burst window, hit hard before they wake


#### Check for lethal

**Step:** 3

**What:** Can the fight end THIS TURN? If yes, dump everything. Lethal turns are free of incoming damage.

**Math:** Sum: hand damage + relic procs + status effects + potion damage. If >= total enemy HP minus their block, you win.


#### Determine block needs

**Step:** 4

**What:** How much HP are you willing to trade to end the fight a turn earlier? Trading 5 HP to skip a turn of incoming 15 damage is correct. Trading 15 HP to skip a 5-damage turn is wrong.

**Principle:** HP is a resource. Calculate the EXCHANGE RATE per turn.


#### Check the Relic Bar

**Step:** 5

**What:** Hover relics with conditional triggers — are you about to proc one?

##### Examples

- Pen Nib — the 10th attack deals 2x damage; line it up with your biggest hit
- Incense Burner — counts turns to a free Intangible; plan around when it triggers
- Letter Opener — every 3rd skill deals AOE damage; count your skills
- Sundial — every 3 shuffles grants energy; plan toward shuffles when energy-starved
- Velvet Choker — caps cards-played per turn at 6; budget your play count


## Play Order Principles

The order you play cards matters as much as which cards you play. A wrong order can waste 10+ damage per turn.

### Rules

- Apply debuffs (Vulnerable, Weak) BEFORE the attacks that benefit from them
- Buff yourself (Strength, Dexterity) BEFORE multi-hit attacks (each hit gets the bonus)
- Draw cards EARLY in the turn to maximize the cards available for spending
- Block cards LAST if you have unspent energy — block is for the upcoming turn, attacks consume energy NOW
- Power cards turn 1 if affordable — they compound across all subsequent turns
- Save situational cards (Body Slam, Reaper) until conditions are met (block accumulated, attack count hit)

### Common Errors

- Playing Bash AFTER Strike (Bash applies Vulnerable; Strike should hit the vulnerable target)
- Playing Strength buffs after multi-hit attacks — wasted buff
- Playing block early in the turn and then having unspent energy at end (block carries to next turn anyway)
- Drawing cards last when an early draw could have unlocked more plays

## Energy Conservation

Sometimes the best play is to end the turn with unspent energy. The cards you'd play would do less than the cards you'll draw next turn could do.

### When To Save Energy

- You have 1-2 energy left and only mediocre 1-cost cards in hand, with a known 2-cost impact card likely to draw next turn
- You're playing Regent and you don't have enough stars yet for a big Heavenly Drill or Seven Stars
- You have a 0-cost win-condition card in your discard pile and you'll shuffle this turn

### When To Spend Everything

- Lethal is reachable (always)
- Enemy has a big incoming attack and you need maximum block
- You have a scaling power you should play (compounds over time)
- End-of-turn effects trigger that benefit from emptied hand or zero energy

## The Draw Pile Anti Rule

The mod exposes draw_pile contents but NOT draw order. Looking at the draw pile tells you what's available; it does NOT tell you what comes next.

### What You Can Say

- 'You have Bash+ left in the deck — keep it in mind for the next reshuffle'
- '1 in 5 chance of drawing Demon Form on the next card'
- 'Your scaling card hasn't been played yet'
- 'The exhaust pile shows Strike was burned — your Perfected Strike still counts it'

### What You Must Not Say

- 'Bash+ is on top, so play Pommel Strike to grab it' (Pommel pulls a RANDOM next card)
- 'You'll draw Demon Form next turn' (deck order is not deterministic at this granularity)
- 'Play Vicious next, it'll grab Bash+' (Vicious is explicitly random)
- 'Hidden Gem will pull your X card' (Hidden Gem is random)

**Why:** STS2 randomizes the draw order on every shuffle. Some card effects ('draw 1', 'draw until non-Attack') trigger random draws from the current deck. Predicting specific cards from these effects is a confident claim about an outcome you can't verify.

## Lethal Recognition

Recognizing lethal a turn early is the difference between taking 0 damage and taking 15 damage.

### Checklist

- Add up base damage in hand (sum of all attack values)
- Add Strength stacks × number of attacks (Strength applies per hit)
- Add Vulnerable multiplier (1.5x to all attacks if enemy is vulnerable)
- Add Weak multiplier (multiply your damage by 0.75 if YOU are weak)
- Add static damage sources (Pen Nib proc, potion damage, relic damage)
- Subtract enemy block
- Account for sequencing — if you can apply Vulnerable first, you ALSO multiply subsequent attacks

**Calculator Example:** Hand: 2 Strikes (6 each = 12), 1 Bash (8 + Vulnerable). Strength: 2. Strikes become 8 each = 16. Bash hits 10. Apply Bash first (8+2=10 damage, 2 Vulnerable). Then Strikes 8 + 8 = 16 × 1.5 = 24. Total: 10 + 24 = 34 damage. If enemy has 32 HP and 0 block: LETHAL.

## Potion Decisions In Combat

Potions are free power. The only cost is opportunity (saving for a better moment).

### Rules

- Defensive potions (Block, Fairy) — use the moment you'd take >10 damage you can't otherwise block
- Offensive potions (Strength, Fire, Steel) — use on elites and boss phases where burst matters
- Utility potions (Smoke Bomb, Snecko Skull) — read the situation; Smoke Bomb is panic-button only
- Draw potions (Cultist, Liquid Memory) — use turn 1 of long fights to set up scaling fast
- Use a potion if it saves more HP than the next potion you'd find on average (~5-8 HP)

## Fundamental Combat Rules

Core engine rules that are easy to misread because they're not surfaced in card tooltips. Getting these wrong silently corrupts every damage/block calculation you do. Verify against these before doing combat math.

### Rules

#### Enemy intent damage is post-multiplier

**Rule:** The damage number shown on an enemy's intent (e.g. 'Attack for 16 damage') is the FINAL value the player will take, already accounting for the enemy's Strength, the player's Vulnerable, the enemy's Weak, and any other active modifiers. Do NOT re-apply multipliers on top.

**Why It Matters:** If the player is Vulnerable and the intent reads 16, the actual incoming damage is 16 — not 24. Re-applying Vulnerable inflates incoming damage by 50%, leading to wrong block plans, panic potion burns, and 'lethal' false alarms.

**How To Apply:** When summing incoming damage from `battle.enemies[].intents[].label`, treat each label as the final number. Multipliers are only applied manually when computing damage YOU deal to enemies (your Strength, Vulnerable on enemy, Weak on you).

**Exception Note:** The intent label captures buffs/debuffs active at the moment of display. If something changes between display and the enemy's turn (e.g., the enemy gains Strength after the intent is shown, or your Vulnerable expires), the actual damage may differ. But the displayed number is the game's authoritative current calculation — never re-multiply it.


#### Unplayed cards discard at end of turn (Retain is the exception)

**Rule:** Every card left in your hand at end of turn is sent to the discard pile automatically. The ONLY way to keep a card across turns is the Retain keyword. There is no 'save this for next turn' by simply not playing it.

**Why It Matters:** Misunderstanding this leads to bad discard choices. When Survivor/Acrobatics/Calculated Gamble asks you to discard one, players often think 'I'll discard the worse card to keep the better one for next turn.' That reasoning is false — both go to discard anyway. The choice only matters for: triggering Sly cards being discarded, feeding discard-count effects (Tactician, etc.), or controlling which cards reshuffle when. It does NOT preserve any card for next turn's hand.

**How To Apply:** When recommending a discard target, the reasons are: (1) trigger a Sly card, (2) feed a discard-count effect, (3) influence reshuffle timing for a specific card. Never 'save it for next turn' — that's not how end-of-turn cleanup works. The 'better' card in hand is just as gone next turn as the 'worse' card.

**Exception Note:** Cards with Retain stay in hand. A few enemy-induced effects and specific powers (Equilibrium, Well-Laid Plans, etc.) can also retain cards. If you're unsure whether a card retains, default to assuming it doesn't.


#### Poison ticks at the start of the poisoned creature's turn, then decrements

**Rule:** When a creature is Poisoned, at the start of THAT creature's turn it (1) loses HP equal to its Poison stacks, then (2) reduces Poison by 1. The HP loss happens BEFORE the creature takes any action that turn.

**Why It Matters:** If your player-turn damage drops an enemy low enough that its poison tick kills it at the start of its next turn, the enemy dies BEFORE attacking — that turn's incoming damage is fully prevented. This enables 'set up the lethal poison tick' plays that look like they shouldn't work (enemy still has HP at end of your turn) but actually save you the whole attack.

**How To Apply:** When checking whether an enemy can be 'killed before it acts,' the threshold is: (player damage dealt) + (poison stacks on the enemy) >= enemy's current HP. If yes, the enemy dies during the poison tick at start of its turn and never gets its action. Multi-enemy fights: each enemy's poison ticks on its own turn, so order of operations matters.

**Exception Note:** Some enemies have Artifact and may negate Poison application. Some bosses/relics modify poison timing. Default to standard rules unless you observe otherwise in the run.


#### End-of-turn hand discard does NOT trigger Discard effects

**Rule:** When your hand is discarded at the end of your turn (the default cleanup), this does NOT trigger cards or relics that proc on 'discard'. Only ACTIVE discards during your turn (Survivor, Acrobatics, Calculated Gamble, Storm of Steel, Shadow Step, etc.) trigger discard-synergy effects like Sly, Tingsha, Memento Mori, Tough Bandages.

**Why It Matters:** Sly cards in hand at end of turn do NOT auto-play — they go to discard like any other card. Discard-payoff effects only fire from intentional in-turn discards. This means having Sly cards without enough active discard enablers is a dead-card situation.

**How To Apply:** When evaluating Sly-based plans, count only active discard sources (Survivor, Acrobatics, etc.). Don't assume end-of-turn cleanup will trigger Sly. When recommending a Survivor/Acrobatics discard target, the choice DOES matter for Sly: discarding a Sly card during your turn triggers it; leaving it for end-of-turn cleanup does not.

**Exception Note:** Some cards/effects may explicitly proc on end-of-turn discard — read each card's text. Default assumption: end-of-turn discard is silent.


#### Unspent energy is lost at end of turn (no carryover by default)

**Rule:** Energy resets to your max (typically 3) at the start of each turn. Any unspent energy at end of turn is wasted — it does NOT carry into the next turn. This is the same as STS1.

**Why It Matters:** Banking energy 'for next turn' by ending early is wrong. If you have leftover energy and any playable card (even a Defend), play it. The block carries to next turn (until your next turn's cleanup), but the energy doesn't.

**How To Apply:** Always spend all energy unless: (1) lethal already secured, (2) playing more cards would actively hurt (Velvet Choker cap, status-card generation from boss like Aeonglass, etc.), or (3) you have a specific relic like Ice Cream that DOES carry energy. The Energy Conservation section above covers when literal save-energy plays apply — those are about choosing NOT to play mediocre cards, not about banking energy.

**Exception Note:** Ice Cream relic: 'You no longer lose unspent energy at the start of each turn.' Pael's Tears relic gives bonus energy next turn if you end with exactly 1 leftover. Without one of these, no carryover.


#### Hand size cap is 10 — drawn cards beyond the cap are immediately discarded

**Rule:** Your hand can hold a maximum of 10 cards at any time. Cards drawn beyond 10 (from any source — draw effects, generated cards, Shivs from Blade Dance, statuses from enemies) are sent directly to the discard pile without entering your hand.

**Why It Matters:** On big draw turns (Blade Dance + Acrobatics + Backflip stacking), you can overdraw and lose cards. Same for Shiv-heavy decks playing multiple Shiv generators in a hand that's already near full. The lost cards don't trigger any 'on draw' effects either.

**How To Apply:** Before playing a card that adds many cards to hand (Blade Dance 3 Shivs, Calculated Gamble redraw), check current hand size. If you're at 8 cards and play Blade Dance, only 2 of the 3 Shivs reach your hand. The third is auto-discarded. Play card-spawners EARLY in the turn (when hand has more empty slots from cards you've played) rather than after blocking a bunch of Defends.

**Exception Note:** Some relics or effects may modify hand size cap. Status cards added by enemies (Slimed, Wither) also count toward the 10-cap.


#### Block lasts until the start of your NEXT player turn, then discards (Barricade is the exception)

**Rule:** Block gained on your turn (or via end-of-turn passive effects like Metallicize) persists through the enemy's turn — that's its purpose, absorbing incoming damage. At the start of your next player turn, current block resets to 0 unless you have Barricade (Ironclad) or an equivalent effect.

**Why It Matters:** Block is a one-turn shield, not a stockpile. Over-blocking past incoming damage is wasted block — the excess vanishes at start of your next turn. This is the core 'don't overblock' principle.

**How To Apply:** Calculate exactly the incoming damage from intent labels. Block to match, not exceed (except by a small buffer for unknowns). The wasted excess could have been damage or a power play. Dexterity makes this even more important: with +2 Dex, a Defend goes from 5 to 7 block — easier to overshoot on light-damage turns.

**Exception Note:** Barricade keeps your block between turns — completely changes block math, makes Entrench/Body Slam viable. Some 'Next turn, gain X Block' effects (Dodge and Roll, Prolong, Self-Forming Clay) bypass the reset because they grant fresh block at the start of the next turn. Frost Orbs generate fresh block each turn end and are not affected by the reset.


#### Dexterity and Frail only modify direct block from cards, not all block sources

**Rule:** Dexterity (+block) and Frail (-25% block) apply ONLY to direct block grants printed on cards (Defend, Iron Wave, Survivor, etc.). They do NOT apply to: (1) block from Relics, (2) block from end-of-turn powers like Metallicize, (3) block generated as a side effect of other powers (Rage, After Image, etc.), or (4) Frost Orb passive block.

**Why It Matters:** Misjudging Dex value: stacking Dex while your block comes mostly from Metallicize or After Image is much weaker than expected. Conversely, Frail looks scary but doesn't gut After Image / Metallicize / orb-based defenses — those characters can play through Frail safely.

**How To Apply:** When evaluating Dex/Frail impact, count only the direct block printed on the card's text. After Image's 'gain 1 block per card played' is not boosted by Dex. A Defect with mostly Frost Orb block barely cares about Frail.

**Exception Note:** Card text is authoritative — if a card says 'gain X Block' (numbered in the card text), Dex/Frail apply. If the block comes from a separate trigger or power proc, they don't.


**Discovery Note:** These rules were added after the coach repeatedly tripped on them in live runs. When you find another rule that's commonly misread (something not surfaced in tooltips, a sequencing quirk, an enemy mechanic the wiki contradicts), add it here rather than re-learning it every session.


---

# Economy

Gold economy and shop strategy in STS2. The economy meta shifts dramatically on Ascension 6+ due to the Inflation modifier — strategies that work at A0-A5 actively fail at A6+. This file covers both regimes.

## Ascension 6 Inflation

On Ascension 6 and higher, the 'Inflation' modifier replaces the older 'less rest sites' modifier. Inflation specifically targets the shop economy: card removals start at 100 gold (up from 75), and each subsequent removal costs +50 gold (instead of +25).

### Removal Cost Table

**Removal 1:** 100 gold

**Removal 2:** 150 gold

**Removal 3:** 200 gold

**Removal 4:** 250 gold

**Removal 5:** 300 gold

**First Five Total:** 1000 gold (vs ~625 at A0-A5)

### Strategic Implications

- The 10-card ultra-thin starter-removal strategy is DEAD at A6+ — you simply can't afford that many removals
- Decks shift from 'thin and infinite' to 'thick and value-dense' (30-40 cards)
- Each draft pick matters more because you can't easily delete mediocre cards later
- Skip aggressively in early acts — adding bloat you can't remove is a permanent burden
- Gold-generating relics and events become disproportionately strong

### Deck Targets A6 Plus

**Act 1 Exit:** 18-22 cards (not 15-20)

**Act 2 Exit:** 25-32 cards (not 20-25)

**Act 3 Entry:** Often 30+ cards — value density matters more than thinness

## Shop Discipline

Shops are limited resources. You want maximum value per visit, which means batching gold and arriving with a clear shopping list.

### Core Rules

- Aim for exactly 1 shop visit per Act — visiting zero wastes accumulated gold; visiting multiple wastes nodes that could have generated power
- Only visit a second shop in an act if you have 400+ gold AND a specific high-value purchase in mind
- Visit shops LATE in the act after farming gold from hallway fights, events, and elite drops
- Arrive with at least 250 gold for meaningful purchases (removal + 1 relic, or 2 cards, or a key potion stockpile)

### Purchase Priority Ranking

- 1. Card removal (always at least 1 per shop, 2 if you can afford and have specific Strikes/Defends to delete)
- 2. Relics with strong synergy to your existing deck (re-evaluate every shop — a relic that was bad in Act 1 may be great in Act 2)
- 3. Specific potions for the next elite/boss (Strength, Block, Smoke Bomb if you're fragile)
- 4. Cards ONLY if they fill a critical job your deck is missing — never buy 'good' cards just because they're available
- 5. Colorless cards if premium (Apotheosis, Master of Strategy, etc.) — these break archetype lock

**Skipping A Shop:** Sometimes the right move is to walk through a shop and buy nothing. If everything is overpriced or doesn't fit your build, save the gold for the next act's shop.

## Foul Potion Trick

Foul Potions ('throw at enemy: lose all gold') seem like trash. They're not — they're a Merchant interaction.

**The Trick:** When you have a Foul Potion, you can throw it AT the Merchant NPC during a shop visit. He gives you 100 gold per Foul Potion thrown.

**Implication:** Foul Potions are effectively 100-gold tokens that consume a potion slot. Always pick them up if you have a free slot, and dump them at the next shop.

**Interaction With File Holster:** If you took the File Holster Ancient blessing (extra potion slot), Foul Potions become even more attractive — that extra slot can be a temporary gold-holding container.

## Gold Generation

### Primary Sources

- Hallway fight rewards (15-40 gold per fight depending on act)
- Elite fight rewards (50-100+ gold per elite)
- Shop merchant 'sell' option on duplicate relics or unwanted potions
- Gold-rewarding events ('Living Wall', 'Pleasure Spirits', etc.)
- Foul Potion → merchant trick (100 gold each)

### Compounding Relics

- Bloody Idol — heal 5 HP every time you receive 100+ gold (effective sustain from gold)
- Smiling Mask — every merchant has 50% off the first removal (massive A6+ value)
- Membership Card — 50% off all shop items
- Old Coin — instant +300 gold at pickup
- Maw Bank — +12 gold every floor up to a cap

### Gold Dump Targets

- Card removal (always)
- Key archetype-defining card from the shop pool
- Relics that compound (energy, draw, scaling)
- Potions before a tough elite or the act boss

## Value Per Node Framework

Every map node has an implicit gold/HP/power value. Pathing is about maximizing total expected value across the act.

### Approximate Node Values

**Easy Hallway:** +25 gold, ~5 HP, 1 card or potion drop

**Hard Hallway:** +30 gold, ~10 HP cost, 1 card or potion drop

**Elite:** +60-100 gold, ~15-25 HP cost, 1 card + 1 relic (huge value if survivable)

**Campfire:** +0 gold, restore ~30% HP OR upgrade a card (often higher value than a relic)

**Shop:** Variable gold spent, potential huge value depending on inventory

**Event:** Highly variable — read carefully, some are amazing, some are traps

**Treasure Chest Act 1:** +1 relic (chest skip optional)

**Rule Of Thumb:** An elite is worth ~1.5 hallway fights of value but ~2-3 hallway fights of HP cost. Take elites when your deck is strong and your HP is above 60%.
